Pregnancy

Sunburn during pregnancy: care, medicines and prevention

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Sore, hot skin after time outdoors deserves gentle care and a check of how you feel overall. Pregnancy adds questions about medicines, overheating and the baby, but it does not mean you must endure pain without treatment. Start by leaving the sun, cooling down and deciding whether you need medical help.

Sunburn and overheating are different problems

Sunburn is injury from ultraviolet (UV) radiation. Skin can feel tender and hot, swell, peel or blister; redness may be less obvious on brown or black skin. Symptoms can appear hours after exposure. Pregnancy can bring sensitive skin or darker patches, but not every rash after being outdoors is a sunburn.

Heat illness concerns the body’s ability to control its temperature. It can happen alongside sunburn or without it. A red patch does not measure your core temperature or establish that your baby has been harmed. If you were overheated, unwell or exposed for a long time, tell your maternity team when it happened, your pregnancy stage and your symptoms.

Tanning is not made safe by water or sunscreen

A UV tan is a response to skin damage. Deliberate sunbathing and tanning beds are not recommended ways to enjoy pregnancy or protect your skin. Sunscreen reduces UV exposure when used correctly, but it does not make unlimited time in the sun safe. Drinking water helps hydration; it does not prevent UV damage.

Significant heat exposure during pregnancy is associated with adverse outcomes, and early overheating research raises developmental concerns. These findings do not predict the outcome of one outing or prove that a mild skin burn injured the fetus. Avoid both intentional tanning and overheating, and seek individual advice about a concerning exposure rather than accepting a guarantee of harm or safety.

Begin with gentle cooling

Go indoors or into reliable shade. Use a cool shower, bath or clean damp cloth to ease the skin, then pat dry gently. Choose loose, soft clothing and keep the burned area out of direct sunlight until healed. Take care getting in or out of a bath if you feel lightheaded.

Do not press ice or an ice pack onto sunburn, scrub the area or peel loose skin. A cool cloth is for comfort, not a reason to postpone assessment of blisters or illness. Many mild burns improve within about a week, but worsening pain or failure to improve needs advice rather than waiting for a promised healing date.

Moisturisers and aloe need realistic expectations

For intact, mildly burned skin, an unperfumed moisturiser can ease dryness and discomfort. A suitable aloe-containing moisturiser may soothe, but it cannot reverse UV damage or guarantee faster healing in pregnancy. Stop a product if it stings, itches or causes a rash. Keep the routine simple rather than layering fragranced or medicated products.

A raw aloe leaf is not a standardised skin-care product, and ‘natural’ does not establish safety. Ask a pharmacist about the formulation and the condition of your skin. Do not drink aloe juice or take aloe supplements to treat a burn: oral aloe may be unsafe in pregnancy. Evidence about one aloe preparation does not apply to every gel, whole-leaf extract or home remedy.

Leave blisters intact and obtain advice

Do not pop blisters, cut away their roofs or scratch peeling skin. Sunburn with blisters or substantial swelling needs prompt medical advice. Keep the area clean and ask whether a nonstick dressing or another wound-care measure is needed, especially if a blister has opened or clothing rubs against it.

Advice about ointments depends on the wound: NHS guidance advises against petroleum jelly over sunburned skin, while dermatology advice discusses it for protecting blisters. Follow the clinician’s specific blister-care plan instead of spreading an ointment over the whole burn. Increasing pain, spreading redness or swelling, pus or fever warrants reassessment; do not use sunscreen as an open-wound dressing.

Pain relief can be appropriate in pregnancy

Paracetamol, also called acetaminophen, is generally the first-choice painkiller in pregnancy when needed. Check the exact product and follow its label or your clinician’s instructions, using the lowest effective dose for the shortest necessary time. Ask first if you have liver or kidney disease, weigh under 50 kg, take other medicines or are unsure about the dose.

Do not combine products containing paracetamol, such as a pain tablet and a cold remedy. Get urgent professional advice if you take more than the label allows, even if you feel well. Persistent or severe pain deserves assessment. Pregnancy does not justify a blanket ban on oral painkillers, but a vague instruction to take a ‘low dose’ is not an adequate dosing plan.

Do not copy general ibuprofen or aspirin advice

General sunburn advice sometimes mentions ibuprofen or aspirin. During pregnancy, check with your clinician before using these or other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), including naproxen. From 20 weeks, do not use an NSAID unless specifically advised: fetal kidney problems and reduced amniotic fluid can occur. Later pregnancy adds fetal heart-circulation risks.

A clinician may prescribe an NSAID in a selected situation with limits and monitoring; that does not make self-treatment appropriate. Prescribed low-dose aspirin for a pregnancy condition is a separate use. Do not stop it because you have read a sunburn warning, and do not increase it for burn pain. Ask about an accidental dose without assuming that harm has occurred.

Check numbing creams and every active ingredient

Do not choose a benzocaine or lidocaine spray or cream simply because it is sold for pain. Ask a pharmacist or clinician whether the exact product is suitable for pregnancy and sunburn, particularly over a large area or on irritated, blistered or broken skin. Damaged skin and repeated application can increase absorption of topical medicines.

This is not a claim that all lidocaine use is forbidden in pregnancy: it has legitimate medical uses, and available birth-defect evidence is reassuring. Benzocaine has less pregnancy evidence. Neither fact establishes that every numbing mixture is appropriate for your burn. Show the full ingredient list, other medicines and pregnancy stage; avoid adding a medicated product while waiting for advice.

Cool the body and replace fluids sensibly

Rest in a cool place and drink water regularly if you are fully alert and can swallow safely. If you feel sick, try small frequent sips. Continue ordinary meals as tolerated; after prolonged heavy sweating, a clinician may advise appropriate electrolyte replacement. Avoid alcohol. If you have a prescribed fluid restriction, ask for an individual hot-weather plan rather than forcing large volumes.

Dark or reduced urine, thirst, weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea or vomiting after heat exposure need attention. Pregnancy increases vulnerability to heat, and medicines can affect heat tolerance. Do not stop regular treatment yourself. Seek prompt medical advice if you are unwell, cannot keep fluids down or symptoms persist; the urgent and emergency signs below should guide how quickly to act.

Know when sun exposure needs urgent help

Get urgent medical advice for blistered or swollen sunburn, or after sun exposure if you have a very high temperature, feel hot, cold or shivery, feel very tired, dizzy or sick, or develop headache or muscle cramps. During pregnancy, a temperature of 38°C or higher, a headache that does not go away, gets worse or starts suddenly with severe pain, vision changes, vaginal bleeding or fluid leakage, severe abdominal pain, whether sudden, persistent or worsening, contractions before term or reduced fetal movements needs immediate maternity assessment. Do not assume these symptoms are just sunburn.

After heat exposure, call emergency services for confusion, poor coordination, a seizure, actual fainting or loss of consciousness, very high temperature, hot skin without sweating, a fast heartbeat, fast breathing or breathlessness. Also call if you remain unwell after 30 minutes of cooling, rest and fluids; do not wait 30 minutes when an emergency sign is already present. Keep cooling while help comes, do not drive yourself, and do not give drinks to someone confused or not fully conscious. You do not need every sign to seek help.

Plan shade, clothing and sunscreen together

Check local UV and heat forecasts, choose cooler times for outdoor activity and take shade breaks. Use a broad-brimmed hat, UV-protective sunglasses and light, comfortable clothing that covers the skin. Cloud, a breeze or a comfortable air temperature does not guarantee low UV exposure. Protection is still useful after one accidental burn; blame does not help healing.

Choose a broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher for exposed, intact skin. Mineral products containing zinc oxide or titanium dioxide may be helpful for sensitive pregnancy skin. This does not mean every other approved sunscreen is proven harmful to the fetus. Ask about a suitable formulation if a product irritates you or you are unsure about its ingredients.

Use the product well and review uncertain symptoms

Follow the sunscreen label, generally applying before going outside and reapplying at least every 2 hours outdoors and after swimming, sweating or towelling. Cover easy-to-miss areas such as ears, neck and tops of feet. Water resistance is not waterproofing, and SPF is not a number of safe hours. Check expiry and protect the container from excessive heat.

Keep burned skin covered from direct sun while it heals; sunscreen cannot treat an existing burn. Bring the product names, exposure time, pregnancy stage, symptoms and medicines used when seeking advice. If the rash is unusual, worsening or not improving, get it examined rather than repeatedly changing home remedies. A clinician can assess both skin care and any pregnancy concern.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Record the exposure, pregnancy stage, skin changes and general symptoms before asking for advice.

Check each painkiller or topical product individually rather than avoiding all treatment or assuming every shop-bought product is safe.

Agree on skin care, hydration and a sun-protection plan, with clear urgent and emergency thresholds.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organise symptoms, exposure details, products and questions for your maternity team. It cannot assess burn depth, diagnose heatstroke, select an individual medicine dose or determine a fetal outcome from skin symptoms.

When to seek help

Seek urgent advice for blistered or swollen sunburn or illness after sun exposure. Pregnancy fever of 38°C or higher, a headache that does not go away, gets worse or starts suddenly with severe pain, vision changes, bleeding, fluid leakage, severe abdominal pain, whether sudden, persistent or worsening, preterm contractions or reduced fetal movements needs immediate maternity assessment. Heatstroke signs, including confusion, poor coordination, seizures, actual fainting or loss of consciousness, very high temperature, hot non-sweating skin, a fast heartbeat, rapid breathing or breathlessness, need emergency help. Remaining unwell after 30 minutes of cooling, rest and fluids is also an emergency; do not wait if an emergency sign appears sooner.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Leave the sun, cool gently and protect the skin while it heals.
  • Blisters or feeling unwell need advice; heatstroke signs need emergency help.
  • Paracetamol may be appropriate; NSAIDs and numbing products need pregnancy-specific checks.
  • Water and sunscreen do not make tanning safe or guarantee a pregnancy outcome.
  • Use shade, clothing and broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher together.

Frequently asked questions

Can I tan safely if I use sunscreen and drink water?

No. A UV tan reflects skin damage. Water supports hydration and sunscreen reduces exposure, but neither makes tanning or prolonged heat safe. Choose shade and protection rather than intentional tanning.

Does sunburn mean my baby has been harmed?

A skin burn alone does not establish fetal harm or measure core temperature. Tell your maternity team about significant heat exposure, illness or a worrying episode so they can assess timing and symptoms. Avoid both automatic reassurance and assuming damage.

What can I do for the pain?

Use a cool damp cloth or cool bath, gentle moisturising and loose clothing. Paracetamol is generally the preferred painkiller when needed in pregnancy; check the product, dose and your health circumstances. Severe or persistent pain needs assessment.

Should I pop a blister?

No. Leave it intact, keep it clean and obtain prompt advice about assessment and protection. Follow a specific wound-care plan if it opens, and seek review for worsening pain, swelling, spreading redness, pus or fever.

Are aloe and numbing creams automatically safe?

No. A suitable aloe-containing moisturiser may soothe intact skin, but raw leaves and oral aloe are not equivalent. Ask before using benzocaine, lidocaine or a medicated mixture on sunburn; the formulation, skin condition, area and pregnancy stage matter.

Can I use ibuprofen or my prescribed aspirin?

Do not start ibuprofen or another NSAID for sunburn without pregnancy-specific advice, especially from 20 weeks. Low-dose aspirin prescribed for a pregnancy condition is different: keep to the prescribed plan and do not stop or increase it for this burn.

When is it an emergency?

After heat exposure, confusion, poor coordination, seizures, fainting or loss of consciousness, very high temperature, hot non-sweating skin, a fast heartbeat, rapid breathing or breathlessness needs emergency help. So does remaining unwell after 30 minutes of cooling, rest and fluids. Do not wait for all signs or delay for 30 minutes if one is already present.

Which sunscreen should I choose?

Use broad-spectrum, water-resistant SPF 30 or higher with shade and clothing. Zinc oxide or titanium dioxide can suit sensitive skin. Follow the label and reapply at least every 2 hours outdoors and after water, sweat or towelling; keep healing burned skin out of direct sun.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
